analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent federal rules letting renters stay in homes after their landlord's foreclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill to make renter foreclosure protections permanent died in committee without a hearing or a vote, and the temporary protections remained set to expire on December 31, 2012.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2009 Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act gives renters facing a foreclosure of their building the right to stay until their lease ends, or at least 90 days' notice to move if they have no lease. That law included an expiration date of December 31, 2012. This one-page bill would simply have deleted the expiration date, making the protections permanent. It never advanced past its referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters living in homes whose landlords lose them to foreclosure. Without these rules, a new owner can end a lease on short notice and force a family to move quickly, often right after their landlord's financial collapse, which was a common experience during the foreclosure crisis.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the December 31, 2012 expiration date in the 2009 tenant-protection law, making its rights for tenants permanent rather than temporary.

Under the underlying 2009 law, tenants with leases can stay through the end of their lease, and tenants without leases get at least 90 days' notice before they must move; this bill keeps those rights in place beyond the sunset.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders, banks, and investors who buy foreclosed properties would bear the cost. They could no longer count on the protections lapsing in 2012, so they would have to honor existing leases or give 90 days' notice indefinitely, which delays emptying and reselling a property.

drawbacks.text: Buyers of foreclosed homes have to honor existing leases or give at least 90 days' notice before a tenant must leave, which slows reselling or occupying the property and can reduce what lenders recover on a defaulted loan.

The 2009 law's protections were temporary by design, set to expire at the end of 2012; making them permanent removes the chance for Congress to review how the rules were working before locking them in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to tenants is direct and meaningful: families in a rented home are not evicted on short notice because of a foreclosure they had no part in. The cost falls on buyers of foreclosed properties, mainly banks and investors, in the form of slower turnover and somewhat lower returns on those sales. The bill was deliberately minimal, so the trade-off is straightforward: a modest burden on property buyers in exchange for housing stability for renters, with the burden falling on parties who had already priced in the temporary version of the same rule.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to the Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 4, 2010 by Rep. Keith Ellison with three Democratic cosponsors and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
Its sole content is the repeal of the sunset provision of the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act of 2009, which would otherwise end the tenant protections on December 31, 2012.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the initial referral; the bill received no further action before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and investors who buy foreclosed properties are better off, because the 2009 tenant protections remained temporary and scheduled to lapse, preserving their ability to quickly empty and resell foreclosed homes. Renters who would have relied on permanent protections are worse off.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2009 tenant protections permanent and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

for.name: 4 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no further support followed.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in a Democratic-majority House
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup and never reported the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, but no vote was ever recorded, so no actual split on the bill exists; the bill died in a committee controlled by the same party as its sponsors.

industries.industry: Banks and buyers of foreclosed properties
industries.note: The bill would have removed the scheduled 2012 expiration of tenant-protection rules, so banks and investors would have had to honor leases or give 90 days' notice indefinitely on foreclosed homes. Their interest in fast turnover runs directly against renters' interest in staying housed.
Investors who buy foreclosed homes cheaply and empty them for quick resale or conversion would face longer vacancy timelines. Their gain depends on tenants being forced out quickly.
